description_full: Steel Dynamics, Inc., together with its subsidiaries, operates as a steel producer and metal recycler in the United States. It operates through four segments: Steel Operations, Metals Recycling Operations, Steel Fabrication Operations, and Aluminum Operations. The Steel Operations segment offers hot rolled, cold rolled, and coated steel products; parallel flange beams and channel sections, large unequal leg angles, and reinforcing steel bars, standard strength carbon, intermediate alloy hardness, and premium grade rail products; engineered special-bar-quality products, merchant-bar-quality products, and other engineered round steel bars; channels, angles, flats, merchant rounds, and reinforcing steel bars; and specialty shapes and light structural steel products. This segment also engages in turning, polishing, straightening, chamfering, precision saw-cutting, and heat treating of bar products. Its products are used in construction, automotive, manufacturing, transportation, heavy and agricultural equipment, energy, and pipe and tube markets. The Metals Recycling Operations segment is involved in the ferrous and nonferrous scrap metal processing, transportation, marketing, brokerage, and scrap management services. Its ferrous products include heavy melting steel, busheling, bundled scrap, shredded scrap, steel turnings, and cast-iron products; and nonferrous products comprise aluminum, brass, copper, stainless steel, and other nonferrous metals. The Steel Fabrication Operations segment produces steel non-residential building components, such as steel joists, joist girders, and steel deck products for non-residential steel fabricators, metal building companies, general construction contractors, developers, property owners, brokers, and governmental entities. The Aluminum Operations segment offers recycled aluminum flat rolled products. The company also exports its products. Steel Dynamics, Inc. was incorporated in 1993 and is headquartered in Fort Wayne, Indiana.

financial_summary: Steel Dynamics, Inc. is a large-cap basic materials business with a $32.6B market cap on $18.2B of annual revenue.
The top line has compounded at -7% over the past three years and +9% annually across the full decade, and a shrinking top line is the hardest headwind any business can overcome.

Returns on capital run at 26% against a 10% cost of capital — a 16-point spread that is the clearest signature of an economic moat, and 15% gross margins are typical of commodity economics where competitors can replicate the product cheaply.

The business throws off $502M in free cash flow — roughly 3 cents on every revenue dollar, which is the owner-earnings figure that actually belongs to shareholders, and cash conversion sits at 1.22× so those profits are backed by real cash.
On the balance sheet, leverage is comfortably conservative at 1.7× net debt/EBITDA, and interest coverage of 21× is fortress-like.
Shareholder yield of 3.7% reflects a genuine commitment to returning capital rather than empire-building, and insiders hold 6.6% of the shares.

sector_headwinds.text: Fragmented industry with below-average profit capture — no moat to protect margins
Carries a 39% premium to sector median EV/EBITDA (confirmed by 1 other valuation measure)
Volatile returns on capital suggest the moat is narrower than a snapshot ROIC implies
Insiders are net sellers (100% sell ratio, net $17.3M) — the people closest to the business are reducing their personal stake
Weakness in commodity prices pressures materials companies
Commodity price volatility and cost-curve position — in a downturn only the lowest-cost producer has a business, and the rest carry the overhead.
Environmental remediation liability — tightening regulations on emissions, tailings, and water use create open-ended balance-sheet risk that grows with each legislative cycle.
Trade policy and tariff whiplash — materials producers are first-order casualties of protectionist swings, and margin gets squeezed from both input and output pricing.

sector_tailwinds: Reinvestment rate supports 26% organic growth capacity — capital is compounding inside the business
Altman Z comfortably in the safe zone — a fortress balance sheet on this measure
Founder-led — owner alignment that often matters more than any incentive plan
21 consecutive years of dividend payments — an operating record that makes the dividend claim credible
Healthy payout ratio leaves room for both dividend growth and reinvestment
ROIC sits in the top quartile of Basic Materials peers — the moat is wider than the neighbourhood
Minimal goodwill on the balance sheet — low impairment risk

sect: Its 8% operating margin is roughly in line with the Basic Materials median (9%).
It earns less of the sector's profit than its revenue share would suggest (0.62x).
It accounts for 1.1% of sector revenue and 0.7% of sector operating profit.
Over five years it has been gaining share of the sector profit pool (+1.6% a year).
The sector is fragmented and competitive (HHI 0.03 across 221 companies in the universe; the top four hold 25% of revenue), so pricing power is hard to come by.
mkt: The shares are in a strong uptrend, up 57% over the past year excluding the latest month, though it has pulled back 9% over the last three months.
The price sits mid-way through its 52-week range, 21% below the high.
With annualised volatility of 37% and a beta of 1.21, it amplifies market moves.
Liquidity is deep, with about $216.4M traded a day.
In past sell-offs it fell 54% in the 2020 crash, 31% in the 2022 bear market and 87% in 2008.
val: The price sits above its DCF fair value of $208 (margin of safety -10%), so there is no valuation cushion.
The fair-value models disagree (dispersion 52%), and the Monte Carlo range runs $132 to $325 (P10-P90), so treat the estimate as noisy.
On multiples it looks expensive against Basic Materials peers: EV/EBITDA 11.6 vs 8.3 and P/FCF 65.1 vs 22.4 (sector median).
Against its own history it is dear: the EBIT multiple sits 348% above its 10-year median.
Earnings yields are thin: an FCF yield of 1.5% (below the risk-free rate) and an EBIT/EV of 4.0% (vs the 8% bar).
The 14 covering analysts target $274 on average, 19% above the price, well away from the model's fair value.
prof: ROIC of 26% clears the cost of capital of 9.8% by 16pp, the mark of a value creator; returns have swung a lot from year to year (CV 0.93).
It runs a 15% gross margin and converts 3% of revenue into free cash flow.
Earnings quality looks solid: cash conversion of 1.22x.
ROE of 13% comes mostly from margins and asset turnover rather than leverage (1.8x equity multiplier).
It spends 0.4% of revenue on stock compensation.
hlth: Leverage is moderate at 1.7x net debt to EBITDA ($769.9M of cash against $4.2B of debt), above the 1.5x gate, with interest covered 21.1x.
No distress or manipulation flags (Altman Z 5.7, in the safe zone).
growth: Revenue has compounded at -6.5% over 3 years, 13.6% over 5 years and 9.1% over 10 years, so growth is decelerating, and it has been lumpy (year-to-year swings of 28%).
At current returns, reinvesting 100% of profits supports about 25.8% a year of fundamental growth, enough to sustain growth.
Capex runs 1.7x depreciation (5.2% of sales), so it is building capacity for future growth.
Its Rule of 40 score is 16, below the 40 that marks a healthy growth business.
Analysts expect 23.3% long-term annual earnings growth.
own: Insiders own 6.6%, meaningful skin in the game, and institutions hold 86%.
Insiders have only sold over the past year (12 sales, net $17.3M sold).
It returns 3.7% a year to shareholders (2.8% in buybacks and 0.9% in dividends).
The share count has shrunk 6.1% a year over five years, steadily raising each holder's stake.
It has paid a dividend for 21 consecutive years, raising it 6.8% a year over the last five.
people: With about 14,400 employees, each generates about $1.3M of revenue, 2.0x the Basic Materials median, and revenue has grown 10.0% a year across its filed history.
That works out to $35K of free cash flow per employee.
The company is founder-led, which often keeps management aligned with long-term owners.
CEO pay is $7.0M (6x revenue per employee).
